title: Spring Caching, Async and Scheduling: Quick Revision
summary: Quick revision notes on Spring's @Cacheable caching with Caffeine and Redis, @Async executors, @Scheduled tasks and thread pool configuration, from mental model to pitfalls.

chapters.title: Caching, Async and Scheduling Mental Model
points: All three features are proxy-based AOP: a call through the Spring bean proxy is intercepted, so the annotated method is wrapped with cache, thread or timer behaviour
Each feature needs an opt-in switch on a @Configuration class: @EnableCaching, @EnableAsync, @EnableScheduling; without it the annotations are silently ignored
Self-invocation (this.method() inside the same class) bypasses the proxy, so @Cacheable, @Async and @Transactional do nothing
Annotated methods must be public and on a Spring-managed bean; private or final-class methods are not intercepted
Cache abstraction is a facade: CacheManager hands out named Cache objects, and the provider (Caffeine, Redis) is swappable without changing annotated code

chapters.title: Cacheable, CacheEvict and CachePut Workflow
points: @Cacheable("users") checks the cache first; on a hit the method body is skipped, on a miss it runs and the result is stored
Default key is built from all method arguments (SimpleKey for none); override with key = "#id" or key = "#user.id" using SpEL
@CacheEvict(value = "users", key = "#id") removes one entry; allEntries = true clears the whole cache
@CachePut always runs the method and refreshes the cache entry, which suits update methods; do not mix it with @Cacheable on the same method
condition = "#id > 0" decides before the call whether to cache; unless = "#result == null" decides after the call whether to skip storing
Example: @Cacheable(value="products", key="#id", unless="#result==null") Product find(Long id)

chapters.title: Cache Providers: Caffeine vs Redis
points: Caffeine is in-process: fastest, no network hop, but each app instance has its own copy so entries drift between instances
Redis (spring-boot-starter-data-redis) is shared and out-of-process: consistent across instances and survives restarts, but pays network and serialization cost
Caffeine config: spring.cache.type=caffeine with spring.cache.caffeine.spec=maximumSize=500,expireAfterWrite=10m
Redis config: spring.cache.type=redis with spring.cache.redis.time-to-live=10m; values need a serializer (JSON or Serializable) and per-cache TTLs need a custom RedisCacheConfiguration
Rule of thumb: Caffeine for hot, small, read-mostly data on one node; Redis for multi-instance or large shared data; combine them as an L1/L2 layered cache

chapters.title: Async Methods and Executors
points: @Async on a public method returns immediately and runs the body on an executor thread; return void, Future or CompletableFuture<T>
Without a custom executor Spring Boot auto-configures a ThreadPoolTaskExecutor (applicationTaskExecutor); core size is 8 by default and the queue is unbounded
Pick an executor by name with @Async("mailExecutor") so slow jobs cannot starve other work
Exceptions in void @Async methods never reach the caller; handle them with an AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler, or inspect the CompletableFuture
Security and transaction context are thread-bound and do not propagate to the async thread; the @Async method starts a fresh transaction

chapters.title: Scheduled Tasks and Thread Pool Pitfalls
points: fixedRate=5000 starts every 5s measured from the previous start; fixedDelay=5000 waits 5s after the previous run finishes; initialDelay postpones the first run
cron has six fields (second minute hour day month weekday): "0 0 2 * * *" runs daily at 02:00; add zone = "Asia/Kolkata" to avoid server-timezone surprises
The default scheduler is single-threaded, so one slow @Scheduled job delays all others; set spring.task.scheduling.pool.size or define a TaskScheduler bean

Pool sizing: ThreadPoolExecutor grows past core size only after the queue is full, so an unbounded queue means maxPoolSize never takes effect; set queueCapacity, and use CallerRunsPolicy to apply back pressure
Set setWaitForTasksToCompleteOnShutdown(true) and an awaitTermination period for graceful shutdown, and in a multi-instance deployment lock jobs (ShedLock) so a task does not run on every node

chapters.title: Spring Caching, Async and Scheduling Cheat Sheet
points: Switches: @EnableCaching, @EnableAsync, @EnableScheduling; calls must go through the proxy
Cache annotations: @Cacheable reads or fills, @CachePut always refreshes, @CacheEvict(allEntries=true) clears; set key, condition and unless in SpEL
Providers: Caffeine = local and fast with maximumSize and expireAfterWrite; Redis = shared with a TTL and a serializer
Async: public method, return CompletableFuture, name your executor, use a bounded queue plus a rejection policy
Schedule: fixedRate = start to start, fixedDelay = end to start, cron = 6 fields with a zone; lock jobs with ShedLock when running several instances
